patient_information: A 34-year-old man who is very wasted with a body mass index of 14kg/m2. He was found to have a new diagnosis of HIV and was highly immunosuppressed with a CD4 cell count of 2/μL.
chief_complaint: A 2-week history of fever and a papular rash.
history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a two-week history of fever and a papular rash affecting his whole body, particularly his face and trunk. He also reported a significant weight loss of 7kg over the last three months.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient lives in Phuket, Thailand. He arrived in Germany three days prior to presentation to visit friends.
vitals: The patient was febrile with a temperature of 38.2°C (100.76°F).
physical_exam: On examination, his conjunctivae were pale. He had a generalized non-pruritic rash, predominantly on his face and trunk, consisting of small umbilicated papules. There was generalized lymphadenopathy, with swollen lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular, inguinal, and axillary regions. Abdominal examination revealed a palpable spleen two fingers below the left costal margin and a liver span of 15cm in the midclavicular line.
labs_and_diagnostics: Initial laboratory results revealed pancytopenia with a WBC of 2.1 ×10^9/L, haemoglobin of 9.8g/dL, and platelets of 110 ×10^9/L. The C-reactive protein was elevated at 150mg/L. An HIV test was positive, and the CD4 cell count was 2/μL. Histopathology of a lymph node biopsy showed multiple yeast-like structures. Blood cultures, as well as cultures from a skin biopsy and lymph node aspirate, all grew Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnosis for fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly included infectious diseases and neoplasms. Viral causes such as CMV and EBV were considered. Disseminated tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, and melioidosis were important considerations. Other possibilities included Bartonella spp. causing bacillary angiomatosis, and fungal infections like cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, and talaromycosis, which can present with umbilicated papules. Visceral leishmaniasis and lymphomas were also considered.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was diagnosed with talaromycosis and started on a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B, followed by oral itraconazole. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) was also initiated. At a 3-week follow-up, he was afebrile and gaining weight. Six months later, he developed a recurrence of cervical lymphadenopathy, which was found to be due to an infection with atypical mycobacteria, interpreted as an immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was disseminated talaromycosis in the setting of severe immunosuppression from a new diagnosis of HIV. The causative agent, Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei, was definitively identified from cultures of blood, skin biopsy, and a lymph node aspirate. The diagnosis was further supported by histopathology of the lymph node which showed multiple yeast-like structures, consistent with the fungus.
